title: How do you guys handle the art pipeline?
author: riccochet
selftext:
I've had some ideas i've been playing around with and seeing if i could make it fun. I have a pretty specific look for the art direction and animation, but i find getting this translated into something usable to be pretty difficult.

I used midjourney to come up with a lot of the concept art, reference designs, etc, and i really like what i've come up with so far, but turning that into something in game has been... challenging. I've been using those reference designs to come up with 3D models through meshy and tripo, but animating those models is pretty difficult, especially for people. Faces, hair, fingers, I haven't had much luck getting these to look and feel right in game. In fact it usually comes back as straight up nightmare fuel.

Seeing the projects everyone is developing here makes me wonder how you guys are handling it. are you doing more manual work for animations and such? are you using premade animations packs? Do you have specific AI tools that seem to be better than others?

comments.author: blackskies69
comments.body: nano banana to meshy for the mesh and then tripo API with a mix of prompting claude for how I want the animations to appear and then it sending that to tripo. For example I wanted my tanks to pop apart like toys, so I told it to send that to tripo. Takes a few tries, but so far I can't complain with the results but I'm going with a simple art style, so temper expectations.

replies.author: riccochet
replies.body: Right. Thats a good workflow. all the animations i'm working on are for people so i kinda assumed that would be the biggest issue. People are hard. :P

replies.author: blackskies69
replies.body: Really? I haven't had a chance to try animating a person yet so I don't know the challenges. Are you using an API for animating? I've had success using an API and cowork to find a good art balance for my game.

replies.author: riccochet
replies.body:
Honestly no. I haven't tried it. Going to try with an API and see how it goes. But what i've been doing is getting claude to try and take a fully rigged model and give it reference images to try and match... and it hasn't been ideal. :P i also gave it some movement animation packs to put my 3D models onto. That has gone a bit better, but it hair and fingers aren't usually part of that so those get a bit wonky.

definitely going to give the API thing a try tho.

replies.author: blackskies69
replies.body: It also helps to pull real world examples if its your first game. For example I had my AI research how toys in the 90's broke apart, and then designed the joints for my models based around that. You can take real world examples and turn it into code.

comments.author: Funny_Business_151
comments.body:
I can't help with 3D, but for 2D I do it a different way that I picked up from another maker. Every sprite is a small script. Claude writes a script that builds the character from simple shapes on a tiny grid and saves it as a picture. The walk comes from the same script, so nothing is drawn by hand.

All the scripts share the same colours and the same light direction, so everything looks like it belongs together. My part is looking at it scaled up and saying that looks off, or sending a screenshot of a game I like and saying more like this. It takes a few rounds per sprite.

I redid the art of my jam game in Godot this way, with small pixel people, and no nightmare faces so far. It won't help if you need the 3D look though.

replies.author: riccochet
replies.body: still a really cool idea. I will keep that for future reference. :)

comments.author: NagatoKami
comments.body: Don't know if it will work for 3d but for 2d what I'm doing is, I find completely free to use (no copyright) assets and then redesign with Claude. For 3d you can try Blender mcp. It's one thing to start from a reference image, it's another from a whole model with mesh and texture. And you could probably find animated ones too. For Blender - Sonnet or Opus.

comments.author: Brettinabox
comments.body: So far ive generated everything to godot code, its a very simple neon shape aesthetic so its not a big deal. If you are having trouble with the software, use ai to discover good practices.

comments.author: pugworthy
comments.body: For 3d I’m using various free models that have licensing that lets me use them. Also I’m learning Blender and starting to create my own models.  Lots and lots of good tutorials out there for it.
